question: Does the Qur'an forbid Muslims from being friends with Jews, Christians and other non-Muslims?
asked: I have a close non-Muslim friend and colleague. A Muslim friend of mine said that the Qur'an forbids friendship between Muslims and non-Muslims, based on the verse that says do not take Jews and Christians as awliya.
answer:
Now, this question I have answered in a lot more detail in other lectures, but again, this needs to be said very explicitly: **this is a complete misunderstanding of the verse.** Allah says in the Qur'an: do not take the Yahud and the Nasara as awliya; they are awliya to each other. And unfortunately, some translators translate this as, "Do not take the Yahud and the Nasara as friends." And therefore some people misunderstand that a Muslim cannot be a friend to a non-Muslim.

And this, of course, contradicts the explicit Qur'an and the authentic Sunnah; it contradicts common sense and human reason and emotions; and it contradicts the lived reality of Islam for the last 14 centuries. Anybody who says this has truly cut off from the Qur'an and the Sunnah and the Seerah of the Prophet ﷺ and the lives of the Sahaba and the entire lived human history. And they bring forth an interpretation that has absolutely no basis whatsoever.

Of course, you can be friends with anybody who will be a positive influence on you. Obviously, anybody who's a negative influence on you, whether they're Muslim or non-Muslim, you should be wary of forming strong bonds with. And of course, acquaintances are beyond your control, colleagues are beyond your control, but a proper friendship, where you go to their house and they come to your house... There's no question that birds of a feather flock together. So we should try our best to form the best bonds with the people that will influence us positively, whoever they may be. And no question, the righteous, the people who are righteous worshipers, who are avoiding the major sins and having good lifestyles, no doubt that is the best for us. But to be a friend to a person of another faith, of course this is permissible.

Allah subhanahu wa ta'ala explicitly mentions in the Qur'an that Allah is not stopping you from having birr. And birr is the highest level of friendship, of loyalty; the highest level of servitude is birr. The parents are shown birr. And Allah says: I'm not telling you that you cannot show birr to non-Muslims, much less being just with them.

And again, as I mentioned in many lectures, the word qist and the word birr are the lowest to the highest in terms of a friendship or a relationship. Qist is the very lowest level: tit for tat. If they're good to you, you're good to them; that's qist. And then birr is the highest level, which is what you show to your mother; that's birr. And Allah says: this entire spectrum, I'm not telling you that it is haram to do that to a non-Muslim, unless that person is persecuting you, that person is wanting to kill you, that person is hating you for your religion. Obviously, if that is the case, then how can you be friends (friends meaning not just acquaintances or colleagues) with somebody who is making fun of your religion, making fun of you? That doesn't make any sense. It's really a sign of a huge inferiority complex.

So what does the verse mean? Again, the verse as a whole means that people of one faith tradition will not be able to find protection, military protection, especially political protection, community to community. We're not talking about individual to individual; we're talking about a faith-based community. At times of crises, at times of strife, they need to be very careful in assuming that other communities will have their best interest and their best long-term goals at heart. Because at the end of the day, every community is concerned about itself, and especially a community that is proselytizing, that wants people to embrace its faith. I mean, we are the same; we want people to embrace our faith. And therefore, if other faith communities are brought in at times of conflict, they're going to have some conditions, they're going to put whatever. And so at this point in time, one needs to be very, very careful in this regard.

And of course, by the way, even then, what we are talking about is the Ummah as a whole, or groups of the Ummah or segments of the Ummah, thinking that their best interest lies in turning away from the help of the Ummah and getting political and military aid from those outside without understanding the repercussions. Sometimes they understand the repercussions and they think that it is the lesser of two evils, and this is something that the hadith allows. In Sahih Muslim, our Prophet ﷺ said that towards the end of times, you and the Romans, meaning Western civilization, are going to form an alliance against a third enemy, against a third party, and you will fight them and you will defeat them. The fact that the Prophet ﷺ mentioned this is an indication it is halal. So it is not even the case that every single seeking of protection and aid and treaties is not allowed.

So again, this verse has been overly simplified to the point of it becoming nonsensical by this ridiculous interpretation that a Muslim cannot be friends with somebody of another faith. What it means is that you need to be extra careful, as a community, in assuming that any other community is going to come without any strings attached. No: every community, every nation state, every faith-based community, when it comes in with military help, political help, is going to have certain conditions or whatnot, and you need to be wary of that. And so don't ever think that you should cut off ties with Allah and His Messenger, or with the Muslim ummah, completely. As I said, at times, throughout Islamic history, this has happened, that you have to get help against another third enemy.

And even on an individual level, this is not forbidden. So, for example, you cannot work for a non-Muslim company? Of course you can. Or you cannot hire a non-Muslim? I mean, the Prophet hired Abdullah ibn Urayqit to be the guide all the way to Medina. And as well, the issue of friendship: our Prophet loved his uncle Abu Talib. Umar ibn Khattab had a mushrik, a pagan brother, who would visit him, and he would visit him. And the Sahaba had a number of friends; this is authentically known, that they would interact with people who were outside the faith. And the lived history of Islam: never has there been a Muslim society except that there were non-Muslims within it, forming friendships and business partnerships and doing whatever with the Muslim community.

And therefore we have to be careful of not misinterpreting the Qur'an. Frankly, it is ludicrous to assert that the Qur'an is saying that you cannot have friends, just casual friends, outside of the faith tradition. I hope, inshallah, that question has been answered.
